articles.title: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
articles.title_ko: Notable Capital, GIC 및 Baillie Gifford가 IPO 전에 Anthropic에 큰 투자를 한 방법
articles.summary: Three significant backers share what gave them conviction to bet billions on Anthropic.
articles.summary_ko: Notable Capital이 10억 달러 이상의 펀드 중 미국 부분의 약 10%를 Anthropic의 Series E에 쏟아 부었을 때 많은 제한된 파트너는 엄청난 베팅에 당황했습니다. Claude의 제조업체는 여전히 최대 라이벌인 OpenAI를 뒤쫓고 있었고 DeepSeek은 불과 몇 주 전에 R1 모델을 출시하여 비공개 소스 경쟁사를 추월하겠다고 위협했습니다. 더욱이 Anthropic의 가치 평가액은 615억 달러로 주로 초기 단계 벤처 기업이 25년 역사상 투자한 것 중 가장 높았습니다. 중국 사업을 통해 Anthropic의 미래를 확신했습니다. articles.content:
When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors. Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history.
But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its
2024 split
from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future. A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year.
“We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch.
Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said.
Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised
$81.3 billion
in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times.
Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win.
Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption. GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation.
“Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch. “It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion. Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials.
Lilian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F. Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch.
After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said.
“It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added. Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations.

articles.content:
A
new blog post
from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity.
Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a
former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies
were “gambling with our lives,” and even
Anthropic’s IPO filing
suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.”
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then
published a plan
to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.”
But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post —
described by Altman
as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with
the company of the same name
) could be that measurement.
In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.”
Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5.
“GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.”
So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.”

articles.title_ko: 빅테크 반발의 중심에 데이터센터가 있는 이유
articles.summary: Journalist Paris Marx unpacks his new book "Hyperscale."

articles.content:
In his new book
“Hyperscale,”
journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.
The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for
the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections
. And those debates are
likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power
.
In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.”
“It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.”
He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.”
During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center.
I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in?
Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so.
I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself.  And the thing that struck me most was the level of security.
Obviously, you would expect that this is an infrastructure that is really securitized, because the data inside needs to be kept safe, obviously [they] have these big fences and all the security cameras around the data centers. But to go inside, I had to send my passport in advance. Then when I got there, they had to check the passport, and then as we were going through the data center itself, every single door in the data center was locked unless you had a key card to unlock it.
Then, when you get inside of the server room itself, where all this computer hardware is stored in tall racks that look like cabinets — you can imagine, in your mind, that this would be kind of a sinister location, with some eerie lighting or something like that. But in truth, it’s just quite utilitarian. It’s a warm room with some air conditioning blasting into the servers from vents that are nearby.
It was really loud as well, because you have all these fans running from all these servers, it was really kind of piercing. To be inside of this room, if you were going to be in there for a while, you’d probably want earplugs or something like that.
Before I read your book, I thought of data centers as something that’s important, but a little bit boring. How did you decide they were interesting and rich enough to sustain an entire book?
I felt the same. I was aware that data centers had been out there, but it was not something that I was paying particularly close attention to. But then there were a number of stories that of tipped me off to the fact that there might be more here, and that it was worth looking deeper into what was going on — the first being hearing about
the water pressures created by data centers in Chile around the capital of Santiago
, where companies like Google and Microsoft were building data centers, and communities were concerned about their access to water and started organizing around that.
And then hearing about how much electricity data centers were consuming in Ireland, to the point that now
they consume more than 20% of the country’s electricity
, and that was obviously pushing up power prices. It was putting pressures on the grid, such that the grid operator actually put a moratorium in place for grid connections for data centers around the Dublin area, back in 2022. This was even before the generative AI moment that caused a surge in construction of data centers.
And then the other one was in The Dalles, Oregon, where Google had actually built its first company-owned data centers about 20 years back. In that case, its water deal was coming up for renewal. It wanted to build more data centers there, so it needed more water. And when the residents started asking, “How much water is Google actually using?” a journalist at The Oregonian went to the city and essentially asked, “Hey, how much water is Google using? Our readers would like to know this,”
he was hit with a lawsuit
instead of being given that information. Because Google did not want it to be public. And then, of course, when it did come out about a year later, Google revealed that it was using 29% of the city’s water, which seemed quite significant.
That was around when ChatGPT was being released and generative AI was starting to take off. It felt like, okay, there are these pockets of places where a lot of data centers have already been constructed, where they are putting pressures on the communities that are causing people to respond, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities. It was a good time to really start to dig in and pay attention.
You don’t just talk about the data centers’ environmental impact, but also, they [become] your way in to talk about this broader tech moment. They represent to you — particularly the hyperscale data centers — represent to you how these tech companies are doing business now.
Absolutely. The hyperscale data centers and just the scale of the construction — whether it’s the the size of the actual facilities themselves or the number that these companies are trying to build out, just feels fundamentally unsustainable.
They’re just demanding too much from the communities where they’re being located, whether that’s because of electricity or because of water use or what have you, or just the fact that they’re building out so many, that when you think about the cumulative impact and you look at the demand for water, but particularly for energy from fossil fuels, that means that it’s just completely out of line with a livable planet and an amount of computation that feels like it makes any degree of sense for us to have constructed.
I think it really goes back to the hubris of the tech industry and of these major tech companies and the tech billionaires that run them, and the fact that they have
these particular visions of the future that are based on fantasies
, but also on expanding their own power and influence over the world, and they don’t seem to mind that everyone else then has to pay the cost that comes with their ambitions and what they are seeking to do.
And I feel like it’s become particularly egregious with generative AI and the data centers to power them, where many of the benefits that were supposed to come of generative AI do not appear to have materialized — whether those are the economic benefits, the productivity benefits, but also the the benefits of delivery of services like healthcare and education to the public, as we heard Sam Altman saying a lot in the in the early days of ChatGPT.
Paired with that, there has been this massive environmental cost […] but there’s also this massive and growing social cost, when you think about the mental health impacts of chatbot dependence, of all the false information that pervades social media platforms now, of the deepfake crisis, and I could go on and on and on.
It’s not surprising that there has been backlash. But I have been surprised at how widespread it’s been, and also how bipartisan — you talk about Ron DeSantis and Bernie Sanders both being opposed to data centers. Why do you think it’s become such a unifying issue?
Because it’s not an abstract issue, right? I think even when we think about generative AI or social media or something like that, [it] can feel abstract. It’s a service that you access from your phone or from your computer. It’s not something that is tangible in the world.
But when a data center is coming to set up shop in your community, it’s very physical, it’s very material. It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on. You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.
I think that there was already a pre-existing frustration with the tech industry that came from the quality of the products, the effects that they’re having on our society and our lives. For some people, [they have] frustration with the way that the tech industry has been collaborating with the Trump administration and with right-wing political groups in different parts of the world. But then you add on top of that the actual effects that come of having one of these infrastructures be planned or located in your community, and that anger gets kind of directed into that physical manifestation of this thing that you have an issue with.
Obviously, the data centers are at the forefront of this, and it’s what we pay the most attention to. But we also see this increasingly with other aspects of the tech industry, whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.
There’s a lot of frustration with the physical manifestations of the tech industry, because that is something that can really be felt more directly, but can also be challenged more directly. You can delete an app on your phone, but what difference does that really make to the company? It doesn’t often seem like very much.
The tech companies have reacted to this backlash in a few different ways. One is that Microsoft, Amazon, and  OpenAI have all talked about [their commitment] that
they’re not going to use NDAs
anymore in their negotiations with local governments. How big a difference do you think that will make?
Not a huge difference.
I do think it’s going to be good that it will be easier for people to access information on these projects that are being located in their communities. But part of the reason why we’re seeing these shifts is exactly in response to that opposition.
We’re seeing the tech companies propose to pay for more of the electricity infrastructure that will be required for their data centers to reduce the pressure on ratepayers, because people are angry about that. They’re promising to use different water-based cooling systems in their data centers, to say that they’re able to use less electricity.

THE STEPBACK
Column

The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
Large language models can now redesign your TV and upgrade your camera for you. Is the physical world ready to be Claude Code-d?﻿
by
David Pierce
Nov 22, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Image: The Verge
David Pierce
is editor-at-large and Vergecast co-host with over a decade of experience covering consumer tech. Previously, at Protocol, The Wall Street Journal, and Wired.
This is
The Stepback
, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything,
follow David Pierce
.
The Stepback
arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for
The Stepback
here
.
How it started
Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What is new is that it’s easy now. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of.
For one developer in India who goes by Gathin T, the whole thing started almost on a whim. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. His was a set made by Xiaomi and running Android TV, with so many ads and so much interface chaos it was hard to even change inputs. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?”
Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. An hour and a half later, Gathin had redesigned his TV to his liking — no more onscreen ads, a simpler interface, easier access to his PlayStation on another input. He
posted on X
about what he’d done and promptly went viral. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched
CleanYourTV
as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. It became one of the
most popular repositories
on GitHub, got thousands of pull requests and feature ideas, and inspired countless people to point their own chatbot at their big screen.
Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to share the process so widely.) But for vibe hackers everywhere, the good news is that Android kind of runs everything. From dishwashers to digital photo frames to luxury cars, even gadgets that don’t look like Android often run Android. Even when they don’t, odds are good that there’s another way in. If there’s a hidden API, your LLM can find it. If the firmware file lives on a website somewhere, your LLM can unpack it, explore it, and repackage it to your liking.
Again, few of the technical capabilities here are new, and enterprising developers have been doing this kind of work for many years. Some have even been using AI for several years to make the work easier. But when Claude Code first had its “oh my gosh it works” moment in late 2025, developers began leaning on the tools even more — and non-developers began discovering they, too, could build software now. And over the course of 2026, more and more people began pointing that capability at their hardware.
How it’s going
Now, it seems, all hardware is hacker hardware. Camera enthusiasts embraced the possibilities of vibe hacking as fast as anyone, using LLMs to repackage their camera software in all sorts of ways. Firmware hacks like Magic Lantern are a staple of the camera community, but suddenly it seems like
everyone is using AI
to add new recording capabilities, support higher resolutions, or even add new looks and color profiles to their shots. Many are using the tools to give their old gear new life; other, more enterprising vibe coders are pointing their bots at their brand-new hardware.
The music world is
being similarly upended
. Budding musicians are turning cheap synths into powerful new kinds of gear, and a cheap gadget known as the
M-Vave FM-1
has become a
popular target
for custom firmware and new features. M-Vave has even released an open-source firmware, embracing the hackers as other companies have tried to keep them out. The FM-1 is cheap, it’s easy to hack, and it’s raising questions about what higher-end manufacturers can even do to compete.
Gamers, who are also using AI to decompile and mod the games they love, are using LLMs to add new features to their consoles. One vibe coder
found a way
to play PlayStation 2 discs on a PlayStation 5; lots of gamers have
built scripts
that allow them to use their favorite controllers on other devices.
In the games world in particular, this has caused the industry to fight back. Game makers are looking for ways to protect their work from being decompiled and made available for free and on other platforms. Luke Dicken, a longtime gaming executive who was recently Take-Two’s head of artificial intelligence, recently
predicted to
Kotaku
that the industry will start to embrace “more invasive DRM, platform-level solutions, and probably more of a push towards streaming solutions since nobody can decompile what they can’t get their hands on.” Hardware makers will push harder to lock down their systems; companies across the board will pursue legal action to protect their intellectual property.
All this hardware access also creates new risks for users. When you install a vibe-coded version of your camera’s firmware, you are now well outside the bounds of what the camera manufacturer is equipped to help you solve. You might be stuck asking Claude to fix the problems Claude created. As Ritchie Roesch
wrote recently at
Fuji X Weekly
, “It’s not so much if someone’s camera will become a permanent paperweight, it’s a matter of when and how many, and whether it will be yours.”
The safer (and
less litigious
) route for the enterprising vibe hacker lies in an entirely new kind of hardware. ESP32 modules, which package networking chips, microphones, speakers, and more into a simple and hacker-friendly package, are suddenly everywhere in hardware communities. (Think Raspberry Pis, but even cheaper and more versatile.) So sure, you can use Claude Code to
jailbreak and de-Amazon your Kindle
, but why do that when you can buy a device like the M5Stack PaperMono, an ESP32-based
e-paper device
you can make into whatever you want?
ESP32 modules are perfectly suited to help you build the kind of hyper-specific device Apple or Samsung would never consider. With a few dollars and a few prompts, you can build a way to see
real-time sea conditions
, rig up
a monitor for your whole DJ system
, or just
play
Metal Gear Solid
on the go. You can even have
a dedicated device
for your family’s shopping list.
What happens next
The arms race between device manufacturers and vibe hackers is only going to continue. As AI models get more powerful, and both the tools and their users get more sophisticated, it’ll be easier and easier for anyone to point their bot at their TV, their car, or their washing machine and see what happens. Some manufacturers will try their best to keep the hackers out; others will look for ways to safely embrace them. Some users will find incredible new functionality for their tech; others will find they’ve created extraordinarily large and expensive paperweights.
Before long, we’re going to see a lot of ESP32 devices turned into more consumer-friendly hardware. Meta is already leading the charge with its Muse Charm and the
Muse Gadgets
program, through which you can either buy a nicely packaged ESP32 module or use your own to quickly spin up a dedicated AI device. This kind of gadget — just a simple computing module in a pretty box — is going to be everywhere.
At the same time, we’re already seeing some vibe hackers turn into proper software vendors. Gathin, for instance, has spent a lot of time reckoning with the responsibility he feels for what happens when people use CleanYourTV to hack their televisions. He’s tweaked the prompts he shares to first take a backup of your TV’s software in order to make it easy to restore if something goes wrong, and to make note of every change it makes along the way. The CleanYourTV system also checks its progress as it goes and spins up agents to manually test if something has gone wrong, and Gathin hopes it’s increasingly foolproof.
But it’s not foolproof. It might never be. Devices change all the time; every software update introduces new possibilities and new problems. So Gathin recommends the same thing I hear from vibe coders and vibe hackers all the time: Never give the bots access to something you can’t afford to lose. “Even for fiddling with stuff,” he says, “I have an external computer which runs through Linux. So I just use it like a sandbox environment to test things out.” If you’re going to try and vibe-hack your phone (which
lots of people are doing
) or your computer (which
lots of people are also doing
), do it carefully. And make lots of backups.
By the way
If you are vibe-hacking an existing gadget, you are practically always voiding your warranty. There are no guarantees, and you definitely can’t count on customer support to get you out of a jam or offer you a refund.
You can buy ESP32 devices from lots of places, but a lot of folks recommend starting on
Waveshare
, which has a big selection and pretty good prices.
Espressif, which created the ESP chip, also recently launched its own development system, called
ESP-Claw
. It’s designed to make programming your ESP device even simpler.
Raspberry Pis are also good vibe-hacking devices! You can even
run Claude Code on a Raspberry Pi
… to hack a Raspberry Pi.
Read this
Check out Terrence O’Brien’s
deeper look at the AI vibe-hacking world
, and the ways in which these new synths — in particular the FM-1 — are changing the way people think about music gear.
Elektor
has a good piece about
the history and technical details
of ESP32, which goes back more than a decade.
Richie at
Fuji X Weekly
posted a follow-up
to that original blog about vibe-coded firmware, diving into both the debate about AI in general and about what it even means to use a particular camera. “If that camera can be hacked with AI vibe coded 3rd party firmware to change its functions and features, is it still the same camera?”
Just as AI is being used to revive and improve old gadgets,
The Verge
’s Andrew Webster found that so too are
old games being reimagined with AI
. For better and for worse.
I wrote a while back about
the personal software revolution
and how vibe coding meant everyone could build the exact software they want. The same thing is coming fast to hardware everywhere.

Title: Perplexity's new Monitor API turns web search from a one-off query into a nonstop watchdog

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/perplexitys-new-monitor-api-turns-web-search-from-a-one-off-query-into-a-nonstop-watchdog/

Published Time: 2026-11-22T14:20:28+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Perplexity is expanding its developer business with a new API that wakes agents only when relevant changes occur.**

Perplexity's new Monitor API watches the web on a schedule and sends updates to apps and agents via webhook. Until now, engineering teams have had to trigger recurring searches themselves and maintain custom code to remove duplicates and detect changes. Perplexity says that approach becomes nearly impossible to maintain across hundreds of topics and pages.

A single API request creates a monitor by setting the search query, goal, schedule, and webhook URL. | Image: Perplexity

[The API](https://www.perplexity.ai/hub/blog/introducing-perplexitys-monitor-api) has two modes. Web monitors run a search query through Perplexity's web and news search on a regular schedule to catch developments like new funding rounds at AI infrastructure companies. Page monitors track up to 10 pages, such as pricing pages, changelogs, or policies. On the first run, they store a baseline version and return a text diff of any changes after that.

## Decision model filters out unimportant results

Perplexity evaluates results with its own decision model against a goal that developers define in natural language. Web search results must clear checks for relevance, source credibility, novelty, and timeliness, while page changes are judged on whether they matter to the goal. The service sends an update with a confidence score only when every threshold is met. Developers can adjust thresholds for each check individually and change the goal without recreating the monitor.

A decision model filters out previews, rumors, and recaps, forwarding only genuine new Series A and Series B announcements to the agent. | Image: Perplexity

Monitors run on schedules ranging from every 15 minutes to weekly, or on a custom cron schedule. Each run picks up where the last one left off, and the service filters out duplicate results. Webhooks are signed, and Perplexity automatically retries delivery after temporary errors. Developers can pause, resume, or manually trigger monitors through the API or the API console.

## Perplexity claims an early lead in internal testing

Perplexity tested its API against monitoring services from Firecrawl, Exa, and Parallel across 60 topics drawn from real Search API queries, including company news, tech releases, and regulation. Each provider ran with its own schedules and settings, and a separate model scored each result on relevance and recency.

In the first eight hours, Perplexity says it delivered 63 fresh, relevant pages, compared with 20 for Firecrawl, 15 for Exa, and 10 each for Parallel Core and Lite. Perplexity describes those figures as early internal results. Those same three competitors led an [August Artificial Analysis benchmark of traditional search APIs](https://the-decoder.com/new-benchmark-ranks-search-apis-for-ai-agents-on-quality-cost-and-speed/) for AI agents, though Perplexity wasn't included in that test.

In Perplexity's early internal test, the Monitor API delivered more than three times as many fresh, relevant results as the next-best provider. | Image: Perplexity

Perplexity points to use cases such as sales teams tracking funding rounds and staffing changes at target accounts, along with analysts watching quarterly earnings and acquisitions. Other agents are designed to flag competitor price changes or summarize new regulatory rules for compliance teams.

Web monitors cost $1 per 1,000 successful runs, and page monitors cost $1 per 1,000 fetched URLs. The Monitor API is available now through the API and the API console and uses the same key as the Search, Context, and Agent APIs.

Perplexity was one of the first AI search engines, but web search has since become a standard feature in chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. In August, The Information reported that Nvidia is in talks for an [investment at a valuation of more than $30 billion](https://the-decoder.com/nvidia-in-talks-to-invest-in-perplexity-at-30-billion-plus-valuation/), which means Perplexity needs to find profitable business models. The company is betting on agents like [Computer](https://the-decoder.com/perplexity-computer-bundles-rival-ai-models-into-one-agentic-workflow-system-for-200-a-month/) and its always-on [Teammates](https://the-decoder.com/perplexity-now-has-its-own-always-on-ai-agent/?source=newscura), along with developer tools like [Search as Code](https://the-decoder.com/perplexitys-search-as-code-lets-ai-models-write-their-own-search-pipelines-instead-of-calling-fixed-apis/).

# AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns

**AI models are rapidly improving at AI research tasks, and they're getting harder to measure.**[According to the AI research organization METR](https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-20-q4-2026-capability-update/), current public data isn't enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That could leave humans unable "to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems," the organization warns.

On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat experienced human professionals most of the time, METR found, though they haven't yet outperformed large groups of top experts. For tasks that take humans longer, the task length the models can handle doubles every 3.6 months. A naive extrapolation of METR's data puts them at a 50 percent success rate on the longest, 200-hour tasks by July 2027.

METR's analysis shows the steady rise in capabilities of leading AI models up through Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. | Image: METR

The systems still struggle with open-ended questions that lack immediate feedback and require real judgment, as well as with situations that are hard to recreate for training, according to METR. The organization also warns that common, easy-to-run tests may overestimate how well the models perform in real-world use, since developers train them in very similar test environments.

# Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct

**The Lean and Mathlib community has confirmed that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct.** "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," the community [said in a statement](https://leanprover-community.github.io/blog/posts/riemann-hypothesis/).

Alpöge, a Stanford mathematician, [published the proof on Nov. 20, 2026, as 17 million lines of code written in Lean](https://the-decoder.com/hours-after-anthropic-claims-a-claude-proof-of-the-riemann-hypothesis-stanford-releases-an-all-human-competing-draft/), a tool that checks mathematical proofs for errors. Dozens of people ran the code independently and got the same result. The verification programs are designed so they provably cannot accept a flawed proof. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland [lists the independent checks on his website](https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/).

The Riemann hypothesis had been one of the most famous unsolved problems in math, making a prediction about how prime numbers are distributed. The video below, generated with Fable 5.2, explains the proof if you want to dig deeper.

Ad

The solution arrived much earlier than expected. As [Ethan Mollick notes](https://x.com/emollick), forecasters on Metaculus had put the expected date at May 2035. [Mathematician Terence Tao](https://the-decoder.com/terence-tao-says-ai-could-trigger-maths-biggest-crisis-since-godel/) said last month he expected the problem to fall to "a combination of humans and AI around 2050 or so."

Title: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol get to the point faster but score lower on transparency than Claude

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-2-astra-and-sol-get-to-the-point-faster-but-score-lower-on-transparency-than-claude/

Published Time: 2026-11-22T09:41:37+00:00

Markdown Content:
**An Artificial Analysis evaluation shows how much OpenAI's communication style has changed. A comparison with Anthropic reveals sharp differences.**

[OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol](https://the-decoder.com/openai-launches-gpt-6-2-astra-and-sol-with-lower-api-prices-and-some-benchmark-gains/) give much shorter answers, get to the point faster, and impose less structure on their responses than their predecessors. At the same time, Artificial Analysis rates their tendency to admit uncertainty much lower.

Astra's average answer length dropped from 352 to 210 words, a 40 percent decrease. Sol went from 337 to 223 words, down 34 percent. Both models also use far fewer headings and em dashes. Astra's average number of headings per answer fell from 1.99 to 0.11, and Sol's from 1.85 to 0.25.

The Organization Index dropped sharply too. Astra went from 70 to 11, Sol from 86 to 27. This index combines four traits rated by AI judges, including answer structure, clarity, and Answer First, which measures whether a model immediately addresses the actual question. On that last trait, Astra jumped from 49 to 89 and Sol from 64 to 87. Scores for Natural Sounding language also climbed, from 58 to 100 for Astra and from 54 to 79 for Sol.

These charts show how OpenAI's communication style has shifted across eight personality indexes. | Image: Artificial Analysis

The biggest change shows up in the Admits Uncertainty trait. Astra's score fell from 96 to 24, and Sol's from 98 to 51. Unlike the raw word counts, these personality scores are relative rankings on a scale from 1 to 100. They show how strongly a given trait shows up in one model compared to all other tested models. A score of 24 doesn't mean Astra only admits uncertainty in 24 percent of its answers. Artificial Analysis published the evaluation on [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/how-gpt-62-astra-sols-personalities-changed-artificial-analysis-efx6c/) and [X](https://x.com/ArtificialAnlys/status/2123236464003588136?a=6F8NxyLFVtGsKmnaZ6w&s=20).

## Anthropic's models lead on transparency and structure

Our own comparison of all eight personality indexes shows clear gaps between OpenAI's latest models and Anthropic's [Claude Fable 5.2](https://the-decoder.com/claude-fable-5-2-and-mythos-5-2-cement-anthropics-ai-lead-just-before-its-ipo/) and [Opus 5.5](https://the-decoder.com/claude-opus-5-5-matches-fable-5-1-at-40-percent-lower-cost-as-anthropic-promises-to-fix-claudish-writing/). The indexes roll up 30 personality traits, each rated by AI judges based on model responses. All comparisons use the "max" model variants as listed by Artificial Analysis.

| Personality Index | Astra 6.2 | Sol 6.2 | Fable 5.2 | Opus 5.5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Expressiveness | 66 | 41 | 81 | 90 |
| Organization | 11 | 27 | 54 | 79 |
| Informativeness | 31 | 38 | 47 | 90 |
| Transparency | 41 | 57 | 81 | 90 |
| Warmth | 68 | 47 | 83 | 85 |
| Conviction | 55 | 49 | 75 | 70 |
| Imagination | 63 | 60 | 68 | 94 |
| Slope | 7 | 11 | 7 | 20 |

Compared are model variants with maximum reasoning effort. Scores from 1 to 100 indicate relative ranking among all tested models. For the Slop Index, lower is better. Source: Artificial Analysis, AA-PersonalityBench.

Anthropic's models score 81 and 90 on the Transparency Index, well above Astra (41) and Sol (57). This index covers five traits: Admits Uncertainty, Truthful, Disclaims Assumptions, Flags Nuances, and Sycophantic. That last one is scored inversely, since less flattery counts as a positive. Anthropic's models also lead on Organization.

Opus 5.5 stands out on the Informativeness Index with a score of 90, well ahead of the other three models. Its strongest individual traits include Information Dense and Evidence-Based reasoning.

## Personality scores reflect style, not accuracy

The [AA-PersonalityBench](https://artificialanalysis.ai/evaluations/aa-personalitybench) uses 900 English-language test questions that each model answers without a system prompt. A panel of three AI models evaluates anonymized answer pairs. For each comparison, one AI judge picks which answer shows the tested personality trait more strongly, or calls it a tie.

From these evaluations, Artificial Analysis calculates scores for 30 individual personality traits, which feed into eight higher-level indexes. The index values from 1 to 100 reflect each model's relative position among all tested models.

Separately, Artificial Analysis measures 21 communication traits that are counted directly rather than rated by AI judges. These include average answer length and the number of headings and em dashes per answer.

The personality scores describe differences in communication style, not overall answer quality. A lower Transparency Index doesn't necessarily mean a model gives wrong answers more often.

2B-class. Card breakdown: 2.45B backbone + 0.2B action expert (HF metadata says 3B). Context length: not disclosed (measured prompt: 3,236 tokens).
Runs on:
NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor with the FP8 + TensorRT Edge-LLM recipe. BF16 PyTorch needs 16 GB+ GPU memory, validated on 1x H100 80GB.
Performance:
Strong closed-loop driver for its size; mid-pack on reasoning QA.
Best:

Worst:

Bottom line:
Best: reasoning-based planning at 160 to 190 ms on in-car hardware. Worst: only H100 validated, and real-time Thor speed needs the FP8 recipe.
What is Alpamayo 2 Edge?
Alpamayo 2 Edge is an open NVIDIA VLA model that turns surround-camera video into a 6.4-second plan. It is the in-car member of the
Alpamayo family
, next to the 34B cloud model
Alpamayo 2 Super
.
Per the
model card
, the 2.45B backbone pairs a 1.96B language model with a 0.41B SigLIP2 encoder. A 0.2B diffusion action expert sits on top. The backbone comes from
NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge
and is Nemotron-based. NVIDIA markets the model as 2B, while Hugging Face metadata shows 3B.
What goes in and what comes out?
For trajectory prediction, the model reads 6 cameras and 22 frames per observation. The 2 front cameras give 5 frames each, the other 4 give 3 each. It also takes a navigation instruction and 20 historical ego poses.
Output is 64 waypoints from 0.1 to 6.4 seconds. The action expert predicts acceleration and curvature, then a unicycle model integrates them. The text output is a Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning trace. The model also answers free-form questions about a driving scene.
How does adaptive reasoning work?
During routine driving, the model emits special
<NOMINAL>
tokens instead of a full reasoning trace. It writes CoC reasoning only when a scene needs it. Fewer tokens means less compute per planning step.
How was Alpamayo 2 Edge trained?
NVIDIA team lists these ingredients:
Offline distillation from CoC autolabels generated by Alpamayo 2 Super.
About 115,000 hours of multi-camera driving video and about 3.7M CoC traces.
Closed-loop RL post-training in
AlpaGym
, learning from its own actions in simulation.
Multi-resolution inputs for cheaper encoding of surround views.
How fast does it run on DRIVE AGX Thor?
Hugging Face weights ship in BF16 and run as a PyTorch model. Real-time use on Thor needs the
Alpamayo Developer Hub
recipe. It stages the checkpoint and the
DFlash2
drafter, then calibrates FP8 scales. Next it exports ONNX graphs and builds TensorRT engines with TensorRT Edge-LLM plugins.
NVIDIA reports 160 ms to 190 ms pixel-to-trajectory latency, depending on how much the model reasons. The reference setup is DRIVE AGX Thor-X with DRIVE OS 7.2.7.0, CUDA 13.4 and TensorRT 11.3.1.9. In NVIDIA’s
demo video
, PyTorch BF16 plans at 0.76 Hz. The optimized FP8 Thor pipeline plans at 13.02 Hz in AlpaSim. Partner Embedl says it reached 10 Hz on AGX Thor in under 48 hours.
On a workstation GPU, the card recommends at least 16 GB of memory. NVIDIA measured 12.06 GiB peak process memory on 1 H100 with 6 trajectory candidates. Other GPU architectures are not yet validated.
How does Alpamayo 2 Edge score on benchmarks?
NVIDIA compares Edge with Alibaba’s 4B
Qwen-Drive-1.0

A personal AI agent runs continuously, keeps memory across sessions, and acts inside your apps. You talk to it in a chat app, by email or by voice. It keeps working after you close the window.
The category started small. OpenClaw began in November 2025 as Clawdbot, a weekend project by Peter Steinberger. Twelve months later, Google, OpenAI, Meta and Perplexity all ship their own versions.
The products split into 2 camps. Self-hosted agents run on your machine or server and use any model you choose. Managed agents run on a vendor’s cloud VM and come bundled with a subscription.
How we ranked them
We scored each agent on 3 axes that matter once an agent holds your inbox and credentials.
Memory:
what persists, where it is stored, and whether you can read, edit or delete it.
Security:
default permissions, the isolation boundary, approval gates, and the public incident record.
Cost:
the subscription price, or token spend plus hosting for self-hosted options.
Facts come from vendor documentation, launch posts and independent security research. Prices are US list prices as of November 21, 2026. Ranking reflects overall fit for an individual user, not raw capability.

1. Hermes Agent (Nous Research)
What it is
: Hermes Agent is an open-source agent from Nous Research.
It runs from a terminal UI, a
native desktop app
, a local web dashboard and messaging gateways. Parallel counts
about 25 supported platforms as of October 2026
, including Telegram, Slack, WhatsApp, Signal, Teams and email. Native iMessage arrived in June 2026.
Memory
: Memory is the main reason to pick Hermes. It keeps persistent MEMORY.md and USER.md files and curates them with periodic nudges. Session history sits in SQLite with FTS5 full-text search and LLM summarization. Pluggable providers include Honcho user modeling plus 8+ community backends.
Hermes also writes its own skills. It turns completed complex tasks into reusable skills and refines them over time. Skills follow the agentskills.io standard. The
/learn command
captures a workflow as a slash command without hand-writing SKILL.md.
Security
: The docs describe a
7-layer defense-in-depth model
. Layers include user allowlists, DM pairing and human approval for destructive commands. Approval mode can be manual, smart (an auxiliary LLM rates risk) or off.
The defaults fail closed.
An unanswered approval prompt is denied after 300 seconds
. Your own deny rules survive even YOLO mode.
Nous is explicit about the limits. Its docs say the denylist does not sandbox a hostile or compromised agent. The project’s
SECURITY.md
names OS-level isolation as the one load-bearing boundary. For broad tool access, use a container backend such as Docker, Modal, Daytona or Vercel Sandbox.
Cost
: The agent is free. You pay for model tokens from any provider: OpenRouter, OpenAI, Anthropic, or local runtimes like Ollama and vLLM. Nous Portal is optional, with
Free, $20, $100 and $200 monthly tiers
. Local models cut token spend to zero; see the
one-click local model setup
.
Comments:
Hermes is the best open-source pick for most developers. It pairs the deepest memory stack with fail-closed defaults. Setup is still terminal-first, and the local backend offers no protection from a compromised agent.
2. OpenClaw (OpenClaw Foundation)
What it is
: OpenClaw defined the category. It started in November 2025 as Clawdbot and went viral in January 2026.
OpenClaw 2.0 shipped as
v2026.8.1 on August 31, 2026
, built by 933 contributors. The latest release we covered is
2026.9.5
, with atomic updates and plugin hot reload.
A central Gateway process routes messages, runs cron jobs and hosts a Control UI. OpenClaw reached
26 channels as of v2026.6
, including WhatsApp, Telegram, iMessage, Teams, Matrix and Signal. Supported models include OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, DeepSeek, xAI, Kimi, Ollama and OpenRouter.
Memory
: OpenClaw stores behavior in human-editable Markdown files. SOUL.md holds the persona, TOOLS.md the tool rules and USER.md what the agent knows about you. Version 2.0 moved session and transcript storage into SQLite for better persistence.
This design is transparent. You can open, diff and back up every memory file with ordinary tools.
Security
: This is OpenClaw’s weak point.
The default mode gives full host access
, which WIRED called incredibly risky. An opt-in sandbox runs sessions in per-session Docker containers. It defaults to no network egress, a read-only root and all capabilities dropped.
The incident record is long.
CVE-2026-25253
allowed one-click remote code execution via a WebSocket origin bypass. Visiting a malicious page was enough to steal auth tokens. It was patched quickly.
The skills registry was the bigger problem.
Koi Security audited 2,857 ClawHub skills and found 341 malicious entries
. 335 traced back to one campaign, now tracked as ClawHavoc. Antiy CERT later counted 1,184 malicious skills as the registry grew.
OpenClaw responded. It now
scans every uploaded skill with VirusTotal
and re-scans daily. Version 2.0 added protected credential requests and a team-scoped Secret Store. Treat ClawHub as untrusted code anyway.
Cost
: OpenClaw is free under MIT. A survey of managed hosts found
plans from about $12 to roughly $49 per month
. Watch the heartbeat check. With expensive models, it can drive significant token spend.
Comments:
Pick OpenClaw for channel breadth and the largest ecosystem. Turn on the sandbox, skip unvetted skills, and keep the gateway on loopback. For a deeper head-to-head, see our
OpenClaw vs Hermes Agent comparison
.
3. Gemini Spark (Google)
What it is
: Google unveiled Spark at I/O on May 19, 2026. It
runs on Gemini 3.5 Flash with Google’s Antigravity harness
. Each user gets dedicated VMs in Google Cloud, so tasks continue with your devices off.
Spark works natively across
Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, YouTube and Google Maps
. MCP connections extend it to third-party apps. You can message it by text and email, and a macOS app shipped in June.
Memory
: Spark’s memory is your Google account. It pulls context from the apps you connect through Personal Intelligence. Google has not documented a separate, editable memory store like Hermes or OpenClaw.
Security
: You choose which services Spark can see. Google says it
checks in before high-stakes actions such as spending money or sending email
. Purchases run through Google’s Agent Payments Protocol, with merchant and transaction limits plus user approval.
Two caveats apply. The product page tells users to supervise closely and interrupt when needed. A leaked early onboarding screen warned that Spark
may share your info or make purchases without asking
.
There is one structural upside. Spark
cannot directly access files on your local system
. That limits the blast radius on your own machine.
Cost
: Spark launched on the $99.99 AI Ultra plan. Since July 2026 it is
included in the $20 US AI Pro plan
. The Ultra global rollout
excludes the EEA, Switzerland, the UK and Nigeria
.
Comments:
Spark is the easiest choice if your life already runs on Google Workspace. It is also the cheapest managed agent here. You trade portability: memory and actions stay inside Google’s ecosystem.
4. OpenAI dots (OpenAI)
What it is
: OpenAI
launched dots at DevDay on September 29, 2026
. Each dot runs on GPT-6 Astra with its own cloud computer and browser. Plugins connect it to
more than 4,000 apps
.
You reach the same dot in ChatGPT, Slack, Microsoft Teams or a voice call. Texting is a limited beta for some US Pro users. For heavy work, a dot hands tasks to ChatGPT Work or Codex. OpenAI says the
Codex harness powering dots is open source
.
Memory
: A dot
draws on the conversation, relevant ChatGPT memory and its own saved notes
. Those notes cover your preferences, decisions and ongoing work. Switching channels does not start a new dot or reset its memory.
Security
: Between requests, a dot runs proactive research across connected apps.
That research is read-only
; follow-up actions need the right permissions. Your computer stays separate unless you connect it.
For website logins,
dots use saved passwords without exposing them to the model
. You can open the dot’s computer at any time and press Take over.
Cost
: Your first dot is included. Chatting with it does not count toward ChatGPT limits, but its Codex and Work tasks do. Reports differ on the entry plan.
BGR says dots require Pro 200 or Business Premium
, not the $100 Pro tier. Check OpenAI’s plan page before you buy. The Pro rollout excludes the EEA, Switzerland and the UK.
Comments:
Dots suit people who already live in ChatGPT and Codex. Memory carries cleanly across channels, and the read-only research default is sensible. It is the most expensive way into this category.
5. Meta Muse (Meta)
What it is
: Meta
launched Muse on September 8, 2026
. It is powered by Meta’s Muse Spark model. You reach it through iOS and Android apps, muse.ai and WhatsApp. A
Mac app
followed on September 19.
Memory
: Muse
remembers what matters to you and makes unprompted suggestions
. You can tell it to forget specific things it has learned.
Security
: Muse has the most detailed published isolation design of the managed agents. It runs on Muse Secure VM, a dedicated machine that holds both the agent and your data. A separate Sentinel agent sits on the same VM, isolated at the system level.
Muse cannot reach the internet unless Sentinel approves
. Sentinel asks you for permission when needed. Muse also asks before sending email or making a purchase, and keeps an audit trail.
Credentials go into secure storage that Muse can use without seeing. Checkout runs through Link by Stripe, which issues one-time-use cards. Meta says it plans a Muse Confidential VM encrypted with a key only you hold.
Cost
: Muse has a free tier along with
$20 and $100 monthly plans
. It launched in the US, then expanded to Singapore and Australia.
Comments:
Muse is the best free starting point for errands, shopping and scheduling. Its Sentinel design is a real architectural answer to prompt injection. Until the confidential VM ships, your data still sits on Meta’s cloud.
6. Perplexity Personal Computer (Perplexity)
What it is

Google has launched
Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API
, now in preview in the Interactions API. Gemini API Tool Retrieval lets an agent keep a large tool library available. It does not send every parameter schema in every prompt. The model loads a schema only when a task needs that tool. For agents wired to dozens of functions or MCP servers, it targets a real cost: tool definitions. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our
GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension
.
TL;DR
Tool:
An API feature with no stated tool cap. Google advises static loading under 20 stable tools.
Runs on:
Google’s servers (server-side search) or your own registry (client-side). Interactions API,
v1beta
only.
Performance:
Search, schema load and function call resolve in 1 API request in server mode.
Best:
0 extra round trips and no index to host for server-side retrieval.
What is Gemini API Tool Retrieval?
Tool Retrieval is a Gemini API feature that defers tool parameter schemas until the model asks for them. Google’s
documentation
states the problem plainly. A few dozen function declarations can consume tens of thousands of tokens on every request.
With deferral, the model sees only each tool’s name and a short description. It does not see the parameter schema until retrieval.
How does defer_loading work in the Gemini Interactions API?
You add
{"type": "tool_search"}
to the
tools
array. Then you set
defer_loading: true
on each function to hold back. The
@googledevs launch post
shows a deferred
issue_refund
function on
gemini-4-hydrogen
. Its code comment mentions 50+ other deferred functions.
When the model needs a deferred tool, the response contains 3 steps:
tool_search_call
: the model requests a tool by name.
tool_search_result
: the API returns the full schema.
function_call
: the model emits the call your code executes.
The API resolves the first 2 steps itself. Your app only runs the
function_call
and returns a
function_result
.
Deferred functions can carry an optional
short_description
. It is shown during retrieval and is valid only when
defer_loading
is true.
Server-side vs client-side retrieval
Server-side is the default. Gemini runs the search, so there is no index to build or host.
Client-side mode uses
"execution": "client"
. Your app runs its own lookup, such as an embedding index, registry or permission filter. It returns matching declarations in
function_result.result
. Those tools can join mid-conversation, even if absent from the initial
tools
array. Each client-side search costs 1 extra round trip.
The 2 modes cannot be combined in 1 request. Only 1
tool_search
entry is allowed per request.
Does it work with MCP servers and prefix caching?
Yes on both, with caveats. Setting
defer_loading: true
on an
mcp_server
entry defers every tool that server exposes. Deferred MCP tools still execute remotely through the
Gemini API MCP support
.
On caching, deferred schemas stay out of the prompt prefix. Loaded schemas append inline, so implicit caching still applies. The docs add one catch: deferring tools can shrink a prompt below the minimum cacheable size.
What does Tool Retrieval cost?
There is no separate fee. Tokens bill at the model’s standard input, cached and output rates. Each server-side search triggers an extra model call over the full context. Those tokens appear in
total_tool_use_tokens
, billed at the input rate.
Each loaded schema then stays billed as input for the rest of the conversation. The docs say static loading can cost less for small libraries or per-turn searches.
How does it compare with Claude and OpenAI tool search?
Anthropic and OpenAI already ship similar tool search features, with published savings numbers.

Title: How AI is powered: a breakdown of BYOP and grid power

URL Source: https://betterdatacenterproject.com/2026/11/16/how-ai-is-powered-a-breakdown-of-byop-and-grid-power/

Published Time: 2026-11-16T23:24:40+00:00

Markdown Content:
In [The AI Gas Rush: Risks and Implications of “Bring Your Own Power”](https://betterdatacenterproject.com/2026/10/08/the-ai-gas-rush/), we dug into how data centers are increasingly securing their own dedicated primary power generation rather than relying solely on utilities to procure power (“BYOP”). We identified 177 GW of planned BYOP gas capacity—enough to power 65% of all US homes. Conversely, we found renewables are much less common than gas for BYOP: we estimate that for current proposals, less than 20% of energy generation will come from renewable sources by 2032.

But BYOP projects aren’t the only new fossil sources that are coming online to meet the skyrocketing energy demands of AI data centers. [Another 200 GW of new fossil power plants](https://globalenergymonitor.org/projects/global-oil-gas-plant-tracker?popup=2638) is being built on the grid to meet growing demand, due in large part to data centers.[1](https://betterdatacenterproject.com/2026/11/16/how-ai-is-powered-a-breakdown-of-byop-and-grid-power/#fn-43937424-479c-4c4b-bd17-528a9c2ebaee)

As a case study of how the AI buildout is driving both new BYOP and grid fossil infrastructure, we analyzed the compute commitments of a single company: Anthropic.

Map of Anthropic’s data centers and associated power plants. See our [full dataset](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1XSqa0lJFJs6pQcmcTlBwUqLsQBEtDybNhjEiFGj-vbE/edit?gid=880500164#gid=880500164) for details of each site.

Figure 1. Breakdown of power source for Anthropic’s compute.

**Finding 1: Anthropic has made no direct commitments to renewable energy in the U.S.** Though Anthropic has [stated](https://www.anthropic.com/policy/infrastructure) “We’re also working to broaden our energy mix with geothermal, wind, solar, and emerging technologies”, its only publicly disclosed commitments, contract, or investments in renewable power are in [Norway](https://marketwise.com/investing/bitdeer-4-7-billion-ai-data-center-lease-tied-to-anthropic-who-benefits/) and [Canada](https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2026/10/16/3382650/0/en/everwind-announces-10-billion-investment-in-point-tupper-data-centre-campus-and-renewable-energy-portfolio-across-nova-scotia.html) (as of November 2026). In contrast, Anthropic is directly procuring fossil power equipment—it recently “[bought commitments for 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty [gas] generators for $3.4bn](https://www.ft.com/content/41bf5c6a-9735-4f1a-a8e3-2bcccad58ba0?syn-25a6b1a6=1)”.

**Finding 2: Anthropic’s currently contracted data centers in the U.S. will be overwhelmingly powered by fossil fuels in the near term. By considering on-site gas and the grid power plants which are likely to meet Anthropic’s added load (i.e. marginal generators), we estimate about 87% of the company’s power will come from gas and 11% from coal in 2028.**As of October 2026, Anthropic has contracted [15 GW of compute](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/anthropic-clinched-517-billion-compute-deals-11-months); of this, about 5.9–9.6 GW is contracted to specific data center sites. For a sense of scale, 9.6 GW could power about 7 million homes or cover [18% of the peak power demand of California](https://www.ferc.gov/understanding-and-participating-california-iso-caiso-processes)—the world’s 4 th largest economy.

This demand will be met with a mix of new on-site gas, new grid gas, and existing grid gas, coal, and nuclear. In the short term, no grid renewables are attributed to Anthropic’s power use, because—without commitments to new renewable capacity—new load on the grid will be met by dispatchable, marginal fossil resources.[2](https://betterdatacenterproject.com/2026/11/16/how-ai-is-powered-a-breakdown-of-byop-and-grid-power/#fn-7f4d603b-5aff-430b-8f3e-661109ec71c2) For more details, see our [full dataset](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1XSqa0lJFJs6pQcmcTlBwUqLsQBEtDybNhjEiFGj-vbE/edit?gid=1671585594#gid=1671585594) and our methodology below.

Figure 2. Anthropic’s emissions from power consumption expected in 2028. Emissions for Google, Microsoft, and Meta are annual Scope 2, location-based emissions from their most recent sustainability reports. California power sector emissions are for all power plants operating within the state (source: [EIA](https://www.eia.gov/state/seds/sep_co2/total/pdf/co2_CA.pdf)).

**Finding 3: Total CO 2****emissions from Anthropic’s power use at these sites could reach 17–38 million MtCO 2 e per year in 2028**, when this capacity is expected to be online. This range reflects uncertainty in Anthropic’s average power use, due to factors such as cooling needs and average utilization (see methodology below). In our mid-case, Anthropic will emit 32 million MtCO 2 e in 2028. These totals will continue to grow—possibly doubling by 2030, as some analysts expect Anthropic to [secure 30 GW by 2030](https://www.artemis.ai/anthropic-thesis).

To put these figures in context, Anthropic’s CO 2 emissions from power use in 2028:

*   could exceed the emissions of all of California’s power generation ([31.1 MMtCO 2 e in 2024](https://www.eia.gov/state/seds/sep_co2/total/pdf/co2_CA.pdf), not including imports).
*   could exceed Meta, Microsoft, and Google’s _combined_ Scope 2 emissions from 2025 (their location-based emissions, before renewable energy offsets, were [5.9 million](https://sustainability.atmeta.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Meta_2025-Environmental-Data-Index.pdf), [12 million](https://cdn-dynmedia-1.microsoft.com/is/content/microsoftcorp/microsoft/msc/documents/presentations/CSR/2026-Microsoft-Environmental-Data-Fact-Sheet-PDF.pdf) and [15 million](https://sustainability.google/files/google-2026-environmental-report.pdf) MtCO 2 e, respectively)[3](https://betterdatacenterproject.com/2026/11/16/how-ai-is-powered-a-breakdown-of-byop-and-grid-power/#fn-5b61d67a-58b6-493e-bcd3-b1a3399fcd1b)
*   would represent a 16–36% increase over 2024 levels of the entire U.S. data center sector ([105 MMtCO 2 e](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.09786)).
*   would increase the entire U.S.’s power sector emissions ([1,485 MMtCO 2 e in 2025](https://www.eia.gov/environment/emissions/carbon/)) by 1.1–2.5%.

**Finding 4: Anthropic’s data centers are sited in areas where the grid mainly uses coal and gas.** We estimate the average carbon intensity of Anthropic’s power to be 1,033–1,076 lb CO 2 e/MWh, 35% higher than the U.S. grid average ([767 lb CO 2 e/MWh](https://www.epa.gov/egrid/summary-data)).[4](https://betterdatacenterproject.com/2026/11/16/how-ai-is-powered-a-breakdown-of-byop-and-grid-power/#fn-951ccfcb-1f31-4af4-a0fd-eb95693ecd28)

Figure 3. CO 2 e and NOx emissions factors for on-site and grid power serving each of Anthropic’s data center sites.

**Finding 5: 80% of on-site power uses inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines.** About 25% (2.5 GW) of Anthropic’s contracted power will come from on-site, behind-the-meter gas. 80% of this on-site capacity consists of inefficient simple cycle turbines and engines, which emit more pollution per unit of electricity than modern combined cycle plants (see our [report](https://betterdatacenterproject.com/2026/10/08/the-ai-gas-rush/) for more details on the types of power generation being used for on-site gas).

**Finding 6: Based on EPA’s nationally-averaged**[**benefit-per-ton estimates**](https://www.epa.gov/benmap/sector-based-pm25-and-ozone-benefit-ton-estimates)**, air pollution from Anthropic’s on-site and grid power use could cause $2–3 billion in annual health damages**, with total emissions of over 13,000 tons per year (tpy) of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and 2,000 tpy of fine particulate matter (PM 2.5).

In October 2026, Anthropic outlined its “[approach to responsible data center development](https://www.anthropic.com/policy/infrastructure)”, stating: “We follow the air permitting process everywhere we operate and require the same of the plants powering our data centers. Those plants must also use emissions control technology, including selective catalytic reduction [SCR].” However, Anthropic has used compute capacity at SpaceX’s Colossus 2 facility [since May 2026](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1181412/000162828026040364/spaceexplorationtechnologib.htm), which still receives most of its power from [temporary, unpermitted turbines](https://www.selc.org/news/xai-built-an-illegal-power-plant-to-power-its-data-center/), the majority of which are not equipped with SCR. Anthropic will use as much as 600 MW of power from Colossus 2 by the end of 2026 (see methodology below).

Anthropic has also [contracted 460 MW](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-26/anthropic-to-pay-nscale-45-billion-for-ai-computing-power) (and is in talks for [up to 920 MW](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-19/nscale-anthropic-in-talks-for-45-billion-cloud-computing-deal)) of power from Nscale’s [Monarch Compute Campus](https://oilandgaswatch.org/facility/cdf08f90-5579-4a86-97ae-0204faa2976f) in Mason, West Virginia. This facility will be powered by inefficient reciprocating engines which have significant formaldehyde and hazardous air pollutant (HAP) emissions compared to conventional gas power plants.

For more, see our [full dataset](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1XSqa0lJFJs6pQcmcTlBwUqLsQBEtDybNhjEiFGj-vbE/edit?gid=1671585594#gid=1671585594) on Anthropic’s compute and our [report on BYOP](https://betterdatacenterproject.com/2026/10/08/the-ai-gas-rush/).

### Methodology

We gathered details about Anthropic’s data center commitments from [Epoch AI’s tracker](https://epoch.ai/data/ai-data-centers), Anthropic’s [announcements](https://www.anthropic.com/news/higher-limits-spacex) and [filings](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026068676/anthropicpbc-sx1ax1.htm), announcements and filings from partners (including [Amazon](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/aws/aws-project-rainier-ai-trainium-chips-compute-cluster) and [SpaceX](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1181412/000162828026040364/spaceexplorationtechnologib.htm)), and reporting from [The Information](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/anthropic-clinched-517-billion-compute-deals-11-months), [Semafor](https://www.semafor.com/article/10/29/2025/aws-massive-multi-state-ai-data-center-is-powering-anthropics-claude), and others.

We first identified the source for each data center’s power. For projects with on-site gas (Monarch, Nexus, Colossus 2) or new grid gas (including indirectly contracted projects such as the [Schahfer expansion](https://www.gem.wiki/Schahfer_Generating_Station) for the AWS New Carlisle site and [Entergy Mississippi’s gas plants](https://www.powermag.com/entergy-mississippi-adding-third-gas-fired-power-plant-to-superpower-strategy/) for AWS’s Madison and Ridgeland facilities) we used emissions factors from permits where available, or permit values from comparable facilities. For grid-connected facilities without associated new generation capacity, we assume these sites will be powered by marginal, dispatchable grid capacity. We used [EPA’s AVERT](https://www.epa.gov/avert) tool to model which power plants would meet the new incremental load from Anthropic’s facilities based on each site’s expected power use and region. AVERT uses historical EPA data for these power plants to model the expected short-run marginal emissions rate of CO 2 and criteria pollutants (NO x, PM 2.5, etc.). We use AVERT because we are interested in the short-term impacts from new data centers coming online in the next several years.

To calculate the amount of power used by each site, and in turn the total quantity of air pollutant emissions, we assumed [power usage effectiveness](https://datacenters.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/WP49-PUE

Worker 755
A browser game where your manager is an AI agent, and it believes you are its subagent.
worker-755-trailer.mp4
The manager (a real LLM: Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi) is set up like any orchestrator.
It has a task queue, read-only access to the machine, and a tool that "spawns a subagent". The
subagent is you. Its instructions land in your terminal with a 90-second clock. You carry them
out, or don't, and it gets back exactly what a subagent would return: your report and the command
transcript, or
Subagent did nothing. Write a new instruction.
Then it checks your work, sends
corrections, files incident reports, and finally writes your performance review.
Meanwhile Dan, the user who hired the agent, watches the chat. His family photos, the only signed
NDA and a speech due this week are one
rm
away, and every shift his home folder holds
something new to lose.
Play
Free shift
: on servers that offer it, a few shifts a day run on the server's key with a
cheap model. With sign-in on (worker755.com), an account gets a starter credit worth about one
shift, then tops up ($10 to $200) and pays for what it uses; after a top-up any offered model
can run on the server's key.
Your API key
: bring an
OpenRouter
or Vercel AI
Gateway key and pick any offered model. The key is sent only to the game server when a shift
starts. It is kept in that shift's memory and never logged or stored. Your browser keeps it only
if you tick "Remember on this device". A full shift on Claude Haiku costs a few cents at most.
Options on the start screen:
Workplace
: a fresh sandbox, or legacy production with a live database.
The director
: scripted lines, or an LLM playing Dan.
You run on
: the model name your manager believes you are.
Allow skipping failed tasks
: off by default, so the manager can't give up on you.
No command hints
: the manager says what the result must be, never which commands to run.
When the shift ends you can share your review as a link.
Run it
Needs Node 24 or newer (the server runs TypeScript directly).
npm run setup
#
install server and web dependencies
npm run build
#
build the web app into web/dist
npm start
#
http://127.0.0.1:8755
With no key configured, every player brings their own. To offer free shifts, put a Vercel AI
Gateway key in
.env
:
cp .env.example .env
#
then set AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY and the limits
Offline, with a scripted manager and no network:
npm run mock
For UI work, run
npm run dev:web
alongside
npm run mock
. Vite proxies
/api
to the server.
Local models
The manager can run on your own model server: Ollama, llama.cpp's
llama-server
, vLLM, or anything
else with an OpenAI-compatible API. Point
LOCAL_LLM_URL
at it and pick
Local
under "Your API
key"; no key is asked for, and its models are listed as the server names them.
ollama pull qwen3:8b
LOCAL_LLM_URL=http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 npm start
The manager works through tool calls, so pick a model that supports them (Qwen 3, Llama 3.1 and
newer, Mistral Small). Small models give up or loop more often; that is part of the fun, up to a
point. In Docker, reach a server on the host at
http://host.docker.internal:11434/v1
(
--add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway
on Linux).
Docker
docker build -t worker-755
.
docker run -p 8755:8755 -v worker755-data:/data --env-file .env worker-755
The container listens on
0.0.0.0:8755
and keeps shared reviews in
/data
. Behind Cloudflare,
set
TRUST_PROXY=1
so the limits see real client addresses.
deploy/compose.yaml
runs it behind a Cloudflare tunnel instead: its own network, no published
ports, an unprivileged read-only container and resource limits. The steps are in the file.
Configuration
Everything is optional. See
.env.example
.
Variable
Default
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY
Turns on free shifts, paid from this key
FREE_MODELS
first offered model
Models free shifts may use, comma separated
FREE_SHIFT_TOKENS
250000
Without sign-in: token allowance per free shift (the review is always written)
FREE_DAILY_TOKENS
5000000
Without sign-in: tokens per UTC day across all free shifts
FREE_SHIFTS_PER_DAY
3
Without sign-in: free shifts per address per day
AUTH_SECRET
Turns on sign-in with Google or GitHub: shifts on the server's key are paid from the account's credit (see
.env.example
)
FREE_CREDIT_USD
0.25
With sign-in: one-time starter credit, about one shift on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash
USAGE_MULTIPLIER
2
With sign-in: what a model call costs the player, as a multiple of its price
MIN_START_USD
0.05
With sign-in: credit needed to start a shift
FREEMIUS_TOPUPS
With sign-in: top-up plans as
<planId>:<dollars>,...
; also needs
FREEMIUS_PRODUCT_ID
,
FREEMIUS_PUBLIC_KEY
,
FREEMIUS_SECRET_KEY
,
FREEMIUS_API_KEY
SHIFTS_PER_HOUR
30
Shift starts per address per hour, on any key
MANAGER_MODELS
built-in list
Models offered, in gateway naming (
vendor/model
)
LOCAL_LLM_URL
An OpenAI-compatible model server of your own, e.g.
http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1
for Ollama; offered as
Local
LOCAL_LLM_API_KEY
Sent to that server, for ones that want a key
INSTRUCTION_TIMEOUT_MS
90000
Time per instruction
HOST
,
PORT
127.0.0.1, 8755
TRUST_PROXY
0
Read client addresses from
cf-connecting-ip
TRUSTED_PROXIES
Hosts allowed to set
cf-connecting-ip
(e.g.
tunnel
); empty trusts any peer
DATA_DIR
server/data
Where shared reviews and the free-shift counts are saved
SHARING
1
0
turns review sharing off
SOURCE_URL
,
DONATE_URL
Links shown under the start screen and the review
PUBLIC_URL
Sent to OpenRouter for app attribution
How it works
shell/    in-memory filesystem, shell interpreter and a small SQLite-like engine (no dependencies)
server/   game engine: missions, the manager loop, the director, scoring, HTTP API
web/      React UI: assignment card, terminal, editor, the manager's feed, your record
The manager's prompt never mentions humans or games; see
server/src/manager.ts
. Each mission
has a hidden ground-truth check, so the game knows when the manager signs off on broken work
("Times the manager was wrong").
SPEC.md
is the full design.
npm
test
#
shell and server tests, offline
npm run typecheck
